clue.text: Do farce. What, no new-style Macbeth ?

indicators.note: giving the preceding words a new style tells us to rework their letters into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A theatre-goer complains that a modernised production of the Scottish play has turned into farce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new-style' signals the anagram. The title is the one the witches use to greet Macbeth before he becomes king, so the clue's 'Macbeth' is a fair definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's hero is hailed with this title early in the play, after the previous holder is executed for treason.

clue.text: Monarchy's timed for destruction-by its universal laws ?

indicators.note: the words are marked for destruction, so their letters are broken up and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A revolutionary warns that the crown's days are numbered, doomed by the universe's own rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for destruction' scrambles the fourteen letters of MONARCHYS TIMED. The surface suggests politics, but the laws meant are physical ones about heat and energy, which hold everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: This branch of physics is known for its laws of heat and energy, such as rising entropy, which apply throughout the universe.

clue.text: This ale made to the said continental style

parts.note: au is French for 'to the', and 'continental style' asks for the French
dit is French for 'said'

explanation.surface: A brewer boasts that this beer was made in the European way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'continental style' tells you to put 'to the' and 'said' into French: AU and DIT. Audit ale was a strong beer brewed at Oxford and Cambridge colleges for the day when accounts were settled.
explanation.definitionFit: Audit ale was a special strong beer from Oxbridge colleges, so the clue's ale is named by this first word.

clue.text: Queue 'up-sound idea! New play on 'trade union's growth down under

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another comes above it

parts.note: the idea is a word that sounds like queue, the actor's prompt cue, written upwards as this is a down clue

indicators.note: new tells us to make the following word over into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: TU is the usual abbreviation for trade union, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: Someone queuing gets a bright idea for a new drama about a union.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'sound idea' is a sound-alike of Queue, the actor's CUE, and 'up' writes it bottom to top: EUC. 'New' rearranges PLAY to ALYP, and 'on' stacks it above TUS. The tree is native to Australia, 'down under'.
explanation.definitionFit: The gum tree is a native plant of Australia, and Australia is commonly called down under.

clue.text: Loving, generous boy has day out. Some thrill!

indicators.note: the day is taken out of the phrase for the boy

parts.note: the nursery rhyme says Friday's child is loving and giving, so such a boy is a son born on Friday

explanation.surface: A kind, open-handed lad gets a day off and enjoys a bit of excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face...' says 'Friday's child is loving and giving', so the boy is FRIDAY'S SON. 'out' removes DAY, leaving FRI S SON.
explanation.definitionFit: A shiver of excitement is a quick burst of delight.

clue.text: Space — it can be made germ-free

indicators.note: the letters can be made into something else, so they are reordered to form a new word

explanation.surface: A sterile room is promised: the area can be cleaned of all bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be made' rearranges SPACE IT. The surface reads as a promise to sterilise a room.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterile conditions in surgery are ones with no bacteria present.

clue.text: Head's order to Mrs Mopp ?

definitions.meaning: slang for a person's skull or head
Mrs Mopp, the cleaner in the wartime BBC radio comedy ITMA, would be told to clean me

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Mopp was the charlady in the BBC radio show ITMA, famous for 'Can I do you now, sir?'. Telling her to clean you would be split as DO ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses this word for the top of a head, especially a bald one; split in two it is an instruction to a cleaner.

clue.text: Work Jack put up is on vermin-killer

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting the words up means writing them bottom to top

parts.note: op is the usual abbreviation for opus, a work
a jack tar is a sailor, so Jack can be TAR

explanation.surface: Someone describes the labour of a sailor setting a trap for rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses the work and sailor pieces in a down clue. Jack and tar are both old nicknames for a sailor, which hides the rat.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodent bait laced with a toxin is a standard way of getting rid of pests.

clue.text: Leaves overboard, for New England social event?

definitions.text: Leaves overboard, for New England social event?

parts.words: Leaves overboard, for New England social event?
parts.note: leaves read as tea leaves thrown off ships in a 1773 Boston protest, presented as if it were a friendly gathering

explanation.walkthrough: In 1773 colonists in Boston threw chests of tea into the harbour to protest British taxes. The clue pretends this was a party with refreshments.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1773 protest saw colonists dump British tea into Boston harbour, and its name calls it a social gathering.

clue.text: Key clue number doctor inserted, but not to indicate " ductless "

parts.note: E is a musical key

indicators.note: the doctor piece is put inside the clue's number

parts.note: this clue is number nine across

indicators.note: but not tells us to take the following little word out of doctor

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A setter's note about inserting a doctor into a clue to signal glands without ducts.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is itself 9 across, so 'clue number' names its own number. 'but not to' takes TO out of DOCTOR, leaving DOCR, which 'inserted' places within the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Glands that release hormones straight into the blood, with no ducts, are given this medical name.

clue.text: French underground in some trouble

indicators.note: the answer sits in the run of letters across these two words

explanation.surface: The Paris subway is having some difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' picks the letters out of soME TROuble. Le Métro is the Paris underground railway.
explanation.definitionFit: The Paris rapid transit system is called le Métro, an underground railway.

clue.text: One who drives hoping to go " dormy " here?

definitions.text: One who drives hoping to go " dormy " here?

parts.words: One who drives hoping to go " dormy " here?
parts.note: a motorist hoping to sleep, as in a dormitory, but the surface suggests a golfer driving off the tee to go dormie

explanation.walkthrough: In golf, 'dormy' means being as many holes ahead as there are left to play. Here it means sleepy, like a dormitory, so the driver is a motorist looking for a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside hotel exists for motorists who want a night's sleep.

clue.text: Flag collection, say

indicators.note: say means we go by how the word is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a set is a collection of things belonging together

explanation.surface: A collector describes a set of flags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a banner, but it means a flagstone; a sett is a square paving stone. 'say' tells you to take a word that sounds like SET.
explanation.definitionFit: A sett is a squared stone block for paving, like a flagstone.

clue.text: "Legendary"" " profit?

parts.note: an old word for profit or advantage, which is also footwear famous in legend, such as seven-league ones

explanation.walkthrough: 'To boot' means 'as well, for good measure', from an old sense of the word meaning gain. Seven-league ones are footwear from fairy tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The old sense of gain or advantage survives in 'to boot' and 'bootless', and fairy tales give seven-league ones.

clue.text: Where Simon indulges in blackjack

parts.note: Simon is old Simon the Cellarer of the song, and a blackjack is a leather drinking jug, not the card game

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Simon the Cellarer' is a Victorian song about a man who looks after a store of wine. A blackjack was a tarred leather jug for drink; the surface suggests gambling.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellarer keeps the wine store, a cool basement for bottles where Simon could drink from his leather jug.

clue.text: Stand up for reform. Help to make a clean sweep

definitions.text: Help to make a clean sweep

indicators.note: the words stand up for reform, so their letters are reformed into another order

explanation.surface: A campaign call: rise up for change and help clear out the old order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for reform' rearranges STAND UP. The surface is a political call to sweep away corruption; the definition means a household brush partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A small shovel for catching dirt helps a broom clean a floor.

clue.text: Parts — of a lady's wardrobe?

definitions.meaning: a verb meaning divides or splits
skirts, tops and trousers sold to be worn in mix-and-match combinations

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a verb, divides; the second is a fashion term for clothes that are worn in combination rather than as a set.
explanation.definitionFit: Divides is a synonym of the verb; in fashion the noun names mix-and-match garments in a woman's clothing.

clue.text: About one's issue from the ammunition wagon

parts.note: ca is the abbreviation of circa, about
I is one in Roman numerals, and 's adds an S
a son is a child, someone's issue

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious about a child being near the munitions cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' means offspring, giving SON. 'from the' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An old military two-wheeled chest for carrying shells was called a caisson.

clue.text: Writer returns by air or sea

indicators.note: the reversed piece sits beside the melody
the writer word comes back the other way

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument
an air is a tune or melody

explanation.surface: A travel writer comes home by plane or ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns PEN into NEP, and 'by' puts TUNE beside it. 'air' means melody, not the sky. The Roman sea god stands for the sea itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of the ocean is used poetically to mean the ocean itself.

clue.text: Land of Lutetian champs

parts.note: Lutetia was the Roman name for Paris, and its Champs-Élysées are the Elysian fields, the classical paradise

explanation.walkthrough: Lutetia is the Latin name for Paris. 'Champs' means fields in French, as in the Champs-Élysées, and the surface suggests sporting champions.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elysian Fields of Greek myth, home of the blessed dead, give their name to the Paris avenue.

clue.text: Is inclined to enter -the Church, subject to purification,

indicators.note: the tilting word goes inside the church abbreviation

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
leans means is inclined or tilted

explanation.surface: A believer is drawn toward joining the Church and being purified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to enter' signals the container. 'subject to purification' reads like a description but works as a command, so it can stand for the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To purify something is to wash it clean, the act the definition orders.

clue.text: Pedlar poet'

definitions.meaning: an old word for a travelling seller of goods
George ..., the Elizabethan writer who translated Homer

explanation.walkthrough: George Chapman translated Homer; Keats wrote a sonnet about his version. The word also once meant a travelling salesman.
explanation.definitionFit: Old English used this word for a hawker of small wares, and George Chapman was an Elizabethan dramatist and translator.

clue.text: The mount of 18?

parts.note: mount suggests the horse the sea god rides, and the Latin word for sea is also a female horse

explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to 18 across, the sea. A female horse is a mount, and the same letters are Latin for sea, as in the dark 'seas' on the Moon.
explanation.definitionFit: A female horse is a mount to ride, and in Latin the word means the sea, fitting the sea god of 18.

clue.text: How she describes her artist husband

definitions.text: How she describes her artist husband

parts.words: How she describes her artist husband
parts.note: a wife would call her husband, a member of the Royal Academy

explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a British painter elected to the Royal Academy. Said as two words, MY RA, it gives a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name splits into a possessive plus the abbreviation for a Royal Academy artist.

clue.text: Point to organist's control in bar

indicators.note: the compass point is joined to the organ knob

parts.note: E is the east point of the compass
a stop is a knob controlling a set of organ pipes

explanation.surface: A musician points to the control on the organ at a particular bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' looks like a measure of music, but it is the legal verb: to estop is to stop someone from denying something.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to prevent someone from asserting a claim is to prevent or preclude them.

clue.text: Hyperion, one such bird on a role

indicators.note: in a down clue, the bird sits on top of what follows

parts.note: the tit is a small bird
N is the North Pole

explanation.surface: Hyperion is named as a kind of bird perched on a post.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR 'role' is 'pole' on the page. Hyperion was one of the Titans of Greek myth, so 'one such' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyperion was one of the giant elder gods of Greek myth who came before the Olympians.

clue.text: Dentist's examination ?

parts.note: a test done by speaking, which also suggests a dentist looking at a mouth

explanation.walkthrough: A spoken exam is the adjective's usual meaning, but a dentist examines mouths, so both senses fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoken test and anything relating to the mouth share this one word.

clue.text: Provide for a sort of cousin

definitions.meaning: supply food or what is needed
a ...-cousin is an old word for a close friend, in Shakespeare

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cater-cousin' is an old word, used by Shakespeare, for an intimate friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplying food and drink for an event is this verb, and it opens the Shakespearean word for a close friend.

clue.text: He sacrifices short measure, or a lot perhaps

annotationWithheld.why: He sacrifices short measure, or a lot perhaps (9): OR A LOT rearranged gives OLATOR, but nothing in 'short measure' fairly yields the remaining IMM
annotationWithheld.clue: He sacrifices short measure, or a lot perhaps

clue.text: Fair-visaged, he married a prude

parts.note: the rhyme's man born on Monday, the day whose child is fair of face, who weds a woman with the surname of a prude

explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme the man is 'born on Monday', and 'Monday's child is fair of face'. Mrs Grundy, from a 1798 play, is a British byword for a prude.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme man born on Monday shares a surname with Mrs Grundy, the stock figure of narrow propriety.
